quote: Yeah. Alright. But I don't have any money right now, so I'll be back in about six months.
stewart_read: This is a near-verbatim match to the schema's 'I can't afford it' trigger, which calls for the flip 'what you can't afford is your current bill.' The rep instead responds with a feature explanation ('we take care of everything up front') rather than the inversion move.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have judged that a hard flip this early, before any rapport, risked sounding combative; the softer feature-first response could be a deliberate de-escalation choice given the cold opening.
coaching_implication: Practice the inversion phrasing as a first-response reflex to cost/timing objections raised in the opening seconds, before defaulting to program-mechanics explanation.

quote: Yeah. But you have a cheaper bill. How much are you normally paying right now?
stewart_read: Rep captures the bill ask at a moment of live confusion rather than waiting for a clean verify sequence, which is a reasonable adaptive move but happens before the mechanic itself is resolved.
coaching_implication: Good instinct to ask for the number; the timing (mid-confusion) meant the number landed without being fully leveraged emotionally afterward.

quote: That helps eliminate a lot of the delivery charges they've been spiking on everybody and and everything like that.
stewart_read: Rep moves into utility-delivery-charge mechanics, which is closer-tier financial/technical explanation rather than the setter's qualify-and-schedule job.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as legitimate curiosity-building rather than scope creep, since it's brief and tied directly to her stated bill pain.
coaching_implication: Redirect this kind of mechanism detail to 'that's exactly what our specialist will walk you through on the design call' rather than explaining delivery-charge economics directly.

quote: who would my question is to you, who would install the panels?
stewart_read: Customer asks a specific, closer-tier install-logistics question; rather than redirecting to the specialist to preserve appointment value, the rep answers directly with in-house install and warranty detail.
alternative_hypothesis: Answering directly here may have been necessary to keep her engaged enough to stay on the call for bill collection, since she had just said she didn't have time.
coaching_implication: Use the escape hatch ('our specialist covers install and warranty details on the design call') to preserve that curiosity for the booked appointment instead of resolving it on the setter call.

quote: The only thing we need to finish up a design for you is we do look at your ComEd bill.
stewart_read: Rep transitions cleanly into the required bill-collection ask right after the mechanism is finally clear to the customer, and successfully gets her to locate and text a photo of her bill live on the call.
coaching_implication: This sequencing — resolve confusion, then ask for the bill — worked; worth reinforcing as the right order of operations for confused customers.

quote: Because this has been hot all winter. This is ridiculous.
stewart_read: Customer volunteers unprompted bill-pain frustration while looking at her actual bill — a live emotional anchor point the rep could have reflected back.
coaching_implication: The rep let this pass without acknowledgment; a one-line reflection ('yeah, that's exactly the kind of spike we're trying to lock you out of') would have reinforced the motivation right as she was looking at the number.

quote: Well, let me see here. This all into your light bill. Might as well pay for solar panel.
stewart_read: By the end of the call the customer is self-persuading out loud, reasoning through the value case unprompted — a strong signal the appointment has real behind-it motivation, not just polite compliance.
coaching_implication: Flag for the closer: this customer is already talking herself into the value logic. The closer should let her walk through her own reasoning rather than over-explaining mechanics she's already worked out.
